title: Edgewood Equestrian, LLC horse ranch: classifying accounts into assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses
participant_role: Accounting associate for a CPA firm helping a new client set up financial records
judge_role: New owner of EDGEWOOD EQUESTRIAN, LLC, a 120-acre Arabian show horse ranch
scenario:
You are to assume the role of an accounting associate for a CPA firm. A new client, the owner of EDGEWOOD EQUESTRIAN, LLC., (judge) recently purchased the 120-acre ranch and wants you to help set up financial records for the company

EDGEWOOD EQUESTRIAN, LLC., raises Arabian show horses. The owner (judge) installed a feed barn, arena, horse stables and horse exercise equipment. The owner (judge) also purchased 20 pure bred Arabian horses.

The owner (judge) would like you to help set up the financial records for the new company. You have toured the ranch and requested that the owner (judge) give you a list of everything the company owns, all debt, potential revenue streams and potential expenses. The list is below:
- Boarding Services
- Riding Lessons
- Horse Show Cash Awards
- Hay
- Grain
- Tack (equipment/accessories used with horses)
- Horse Cleaning Supplies (shampoos, shine sprays, fly sprays)
- Grounds Keeper Salary
- Twenty Arabian Horses
- Ranch Hand Wages
- Pitchforks/Shovels
- Horse Exercise Equipment
- Horse Stables
- Feed Barn
- Land
- Mortgage
- Line of Credit
- Cash
- Investments

The owner (judge) wants you to:
- Classify the above accounts into: Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Revenue and Expenses
- Explain the classifications you have chosen for each
- Discuss/Suggest any accounts the owner (judge) might have missed

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Classify the above accounts into: Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Revenue and Expenses

solution.overview: A strong answer sorts the owner's 19 items into the five account types (three revenue streams, feed, supplies, tools and labor as expenses, horses, buildings, equipment, land, cash and investments as assets, mortgage and line of credit as liabilities), defines each type in plain terms, notes that no equity account was listed, and suggests missing accounts such as Owner's Capital, Retained Earnings, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable and Accumulated Depreciation. It also asks the owner follow-up questions and proposes a regular financial review schedule.

answer: Revenue: Boarding Services Income, Riding Lesson Income, Horse Show Cash Awards
Expenses: Hay, Grain, Horse Cleaning Supplies, Grounds Keeper Salary, Ranch Hand Wages, Pitchforks/Shovels, and Tack (unless it is costly and long-lived, in which case it is an asset)
Assets: Cash, Investments, Twenty Arabian Horses, Horse Exercise Equipment, Horse Stables, Feed Barn, Land (the arena would be an asset too)
Liabilities: Mortgage, Line of Credit
Equity: nothing on the owner's list; this is the first gap to point out
Assets are things the company owns that provide a future benefit: the horses, buildings, equipment, land, cash and investments will be used for years
Liabilities are debts or obligations: the mortgage on the ranch and the line of credit must be repaid
Equity is the owner's financial interest in the company: assets minus liabilities
Revenue is the sale of goods or services: boarding, lessons and show winnings bring money in
Expenses are the costs of selling goods or services: feed, supplies, small tools and wages are used up quickly, so they are expensed
Accounting is the process of recording, classifying and summarizing these transactions so the owner can see how the ranch is doing; a chart of accounts organizes them

by_task.task: Accounts the owner might have missed
answer: Owner's Capital (equity): the owner's investment in the LLC
Retained Earnings (equity): profit kept in the company and not paid out to the owner
Accounts Payable (liability): unpaid bills such as taxes and salaries owed
Accounts Receivable (asset): boarding and lesson fees billed to customers but not yet collected
Accumulated Depreciation (contra asset) and Depreciation Expense for the barn, stables, arena and equipment
Others to ask about: the arena as an asset, Interest Expense on the mortgage and line of credit, Utilities, Insurance, Veterinary Expense, Property Taxes, Payroll Taxes Payable

judge_question_answers.question: How does ethics apply to accounting?
answer: Accountants must record transactions honestly and accurately, following GAAP, so the financial statements can be trusted by the owner, lenders and the IRS
Ethics means not hiding debts, inflating assets or revenue, or mixing the owner's personal spending with company records
Confidentiality of the client's information and independence from pressure to make results look better are part of the CPA's professional code
Accurate records keep the ranch compliant with tax law and support good decisions

judge_question_answers.question: How often should we meet to discuss finances?
answer: Meet monthly during the first year to review the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, since the ranch is brand new
Hold a deeper quarterly review for estimated taxes and budgeting, and an annual meeting for year-end statements and the tax return
Meet sooner whenever a major event happens, such as buying more horses, a large show award or drawing on the line of credit

key_concepts.definition: The process of recording, classifying, summarizing and reporting a business's financial transactions so owners and others can make decisions.
A list of all accounts a business uses, organized into assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses, usually with account numbers.
Something the company owns that provides a future benefit, such as cash, horses, stables, land, equipment or investments.
A debt or obligation the company owes, such as a mortgage, a line of credit or accounts payable.
The owner's financial interest in the company. Equity = Assets - Liabilities; includes Owner's Capital and Retained Earnings.
Money earned from selling goods or services, such as boarding fees, riding lessons and horse show cash awards.
The cost of selling goods or services, such as hay, grain, supplies and wages; expenses reduce net income.
Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Every transaction keeps this equation in balance.

Small, short-lived purchases (pitchforks, cleaning supplies) are expensed; costly, long-lived items (stables, exercise equipment, possibly tack) are recorded as assets and depreciated over their useful life.
Profit kept in the company and not paid out to the owner; an equity account.
An account that offsets a plant asset to show how much of its cost has been used up. Book value = Cost - Accumulated Depreciation.
A pre-approved loan a business can draw on as needed; the amount drawn is a liability.
